title: Dolphins at Daybreak

Jack stared out the kitchen window.
The sun was not up yet, but the sky was growing lighter.
Jack had been awake for a long time.
He had been thinking about the dream he'd had.
The dream about Morgan Le Fay.
"The treehouse is back," Morgan had said.
Jack wished the dreams were real.
"Jack!" His little sister Annie appeared in the doorway.
"We have to go to the woods now," she said.
"I had a dream about Morgan," exclaimed Annie.
"She said the treehouse is back, and she's waiting for us."
"She told you to, so it must be important."
"Some dreams aren't, but this one is," said Annie.
"I'll see you later. Wait, wait, I'm coming," said Jack.
Having the same dream must mean something, he thought.
He grabbed his backpack and threw his notebook and pencil into it.
"We'll be back soon, Mom," Jack called into the living room.
"Where are you going so early?" His dad called.
"Just for a quick walk," said Jack.
"It rained last night," called his mom.
"Don't get your shoes wet. We won't."
Jack and Annie ran up their quiet street to the Frog Creek woods.
Soon they came to the tallest oak in the woods.
There was a wooden house high in the treetop.
Someone looked out the window of the treehouse,
a lovely old woman with long white hair.
Jack and Annie climbed up the rope ladder and into the treehouse.
In the dawn light they stared at Morgan Le Fay.
She looked beautiful in a red velvet robe.
Jack pushed his glasses into place.
"We both had dreams about you," said Annie.
"Yes, I sent them to you," said Morgan.
“Merlin the Magician has been up to his tricks again,” said Morgan.
“So I haven’t had any time to collect books for Camelot’s library.”
“Yes, but in order to gather books through time you must be Master Librarians,” said Morgan.
“But you can become Master Librarians,” said Morgan, “if you pass the test.”
“You must show that you know how to do research,” said Morgan, “and show that you can find answers to hard questions.”
She reached into the folds of her robe and pulled out a rolled-up paper.
“The first riddle is written on this ancient scroll,” she said.
“This book will help you find the answer.”
On the cover were the words Ocean Guide.
“This is where you have to go,” said Morgan.
“How will we know if we’ve found the right answer to the riddle?”
Jack let go of Annie’s hand.
She pointed again at the cover and finished her wish: “I wish we could go there.”
Before Morgan could answer, the tree house started to spin.
The tree house spun faster and faster.
Only the ancient scroll and the ocean book were left in her place.
A breeze blew through the window.
Annie picked up the riddle scroll.
Together she and Jack read the riddle: Rough and gray as rock, I’m plain as plain can be.
But hidden deep inside There’s great beauty in me.
“Let’s go find the answer,” said Annie.
She and Jack looked out the window.
The tree house wasn’t in a tree.
“I’m going to do a little research first,” said Jack.
Annie climbed out of the tree house.
Jack picked up the ocean book and flipped through it.
He found a picture of a pink island surrounded by water.
He read: This is a coral reef.
After they die, their skeletons remain.
Over time, the reef builds up from stacks of coral skeletons.
He pulled out his notebook and wrote: “Jack!
Come look at this,” cried Annie.
Jack threw his notebook and the ocean book into his pack.
“Is it the answer to the riddle?”
It doesn’t look very plain,” said Annie.
She was standing at the edge of the water.
Beside her was a strange-looking machine.
Jack hurried over the bumpy coral to get a better look.
The machine was half on the reef and half in the clear blue water.
It looked like a huge white bubble with a big window.
“Is it a special kind of boat?”
Jack found a picture of the machine in the ocean book.
He read: Scientists who study the ocean are called oceanographers.
Sometimes they travel in small diving vessels called submersibles, or “mini-subs,” to study the ocean floor.
Actually, he did want to see what the sub looked like inside.
“It might help us figure out the riddle.”
But we have to be careful.
“And take off your shoes so they won’t get wet,” said Jack.
He and Annie slipped off their shoes and socks and threw them toward the tree house.
Then they stepped carefully over the sharp coral.
Annie turned the handle on the hatch of the mini-sub.
Two seats faced the big window.
In front of the seats was a computer built into a control panel.
Jack opened the ocean book and read more on the mini-sub page: Mini-subs have strong hulls to keep air in and protect those aboard from water pressure.
Computers are used to guide the mini-sub through the ocean.
Annie was waving her hands in front of the computer.
Now the screen showed a map.
“I just pressed a few keys—” said Annie.
I said not to touch anything!”
He and Annie scrambled for the hatch.
The mini-sub slid off the reef.
Then it dove silently down into the deep.
We have to figure this out!”
He saw a row of pictures at the top of the screen.
“I just pressed the ON button,” said Annie.
“That must be the command to go under the water,” said Jack.
Then the map came on,” said Annie.
The map shows the reef,” said Jack.
There’s the mini-sub on the map!
It’s moving away from the reef.”
“It’s like a video game,” said Annie.
“I bet I know what to do.”
Annie pressed a key with an arrow pointing right.
The mini-sub on the screen moved right.
The real mini-sub turned to the right, also.
“You press the arrows to steer the mini-sub.
"You pressed the arrows to steer the minisub, so now we can go back."
So now we can go back.”
“Oh, no, not right away,” said Annie.
“We have to get back to the reef,” said Jack.
His eyes were still glued to the computer screen.
“What if the owners find it gone?”
He pushed his glasses into place and looked up.
Outside the glass was a strange world of bright moving color.
The mini-sub was moving past red, yellow, and blue coral—past little coral mountains, valleys, and caves— past fishes of every color and size.
The answer to Morgan’s riddle must be here,” said Annie.
She might be right, he thought.
Besides, when would they ever get to visit a place like this again?
There were fish everywhere: floating over the swaying sea grass, eating on the white sandy bottom, peeping out of coral caves.
Some kinds of coral looked like blue fingers or lacy fans.
Others looked like deer antlers or lettuce leaves or mushrooms or trees.
Jack read in the book: Coral reefs are only found in warm, tropical waters.
Nearly 5,000 different species of fish live around coral reefs in the Indian and Pacific Oceans.
Jack pulled out his pencil and notebook.
He started to write a list.
The sub floated past a huge starfish.
Jack added to his list: “What is that?”
Jack saw a creature that looked like a giant pancake with a long tail.
He put that on his list as well.
She pointed at the biggest shell Jack had ever seen.
It was as big as a footstool.
“I’ll have to check on that one,” said Jack.
He turned the pages of the ocean book.
When he got to the page about clams, he read aloud: The giant clam of the coral reef is three feet wide and weighs up to 200 pounds.
He added “giant clam” to his list.
Two dolphins were peering in the window.
They tapped their noses against the glass.
“It’s like we’re in a fish tank—and they’re looking at us,” he said.
“Their names are Sukie and Sam,” said Annie.
“Here’s a kiss for you, Sukie,” Annie said.
She pressed her lips to the glass as if she were kissing the dolphin’s nose.
But the dolphin opened her mouth and tossed her head.
“Hey, I know the answer to the riddle—dolphins!”
But they have great beauty inside.”
“You forgot the ‘rough as a rock’ part,” said Jack.
They swam off into the light blue water.
“It’s time for us to go, too,” said Jack.
He was afraid someone might be looking for the mini-sub.
“But we haven’t solved the riddle,” said Annie.
Jack studied the bright underwater world.
“I don’t see the answer,” he said.
“There’s nothing plain at all out there.”
“Then maybe the answer’s in the mini-sub,” said Annie.
They looked around the tiny space.
He studied the row of pictures at the top of the screen.
The words SHIP’S LOG flashed onto the screen.
“It’s a diary of an ocean trip,” said Jack.
He peered at the computer screen and read a log entry: MONDAY, JULY 5 “Hey, that was just last week,” said Jack.
He read further: COLLECTED ROCK AND SHELL SAMPLES MAPPED OCEAN FLOOR FOUND TINY CRACK IN HULL “This is like your notebook,” said Annie.
“Yeah, the oceanographer was writing notes on the computer,” said Jack.
Jack and Annie read further: TUESDAY, JULY 6 CRACK HAS WIDENED MUST RETURN TO REEF SOON “A crack where?”
He read further: WEDNESDAY, JULY 7 MORE TINY CRACKS CANNOT BE FIXED HEADING BACK TO REEF TODAY “Uh-oh.
This doesn’t sound good,” said Jack.
He read further: THURSDAY, JULY 8 DEFECTIVE SUB RETURN TO REEF LEAVE FOR HELICOPTER TO TRANSPORT TO JUNKYARD “ ‘Defective’ means broken, right?”
“And it was waiting to be taken away by a helicopter.
“Now we really have to get back,” said Jack.
“Let’s try pressing the waves picture,” said Annie.
She pressed the waves picture on the computer screen.
The mini-sub began to rise slowly.
The sub went past a small coral mountain.
It went past schools of fish and waving plants.
Two eyes were staring out from behind a giant sea plant.
They looked human—except they were as big as golf balls.
The sub moved past the giant plant.
Jack breathed a sigh of relief.
They stared back at the plant.
Just then, a long arm came out from behind it.
Then another—and another—and another—and another—and another—and another!
Jack and Annie stared in horror at a giant octopus.
Slowly, the octopus crept through the water.
Its eight arms reached for the mini-sub.
Each of its eight arms had two rows of suckers.
The suckers stuck to the window.
The octopus stared at Jack and Annie with huge, human-like eyes.
“I don’t think it wants to hurt us,” whispered Annie.
“I—I’m going to research it,” said Jack.
His hands shook as he flipped through the pages of the ocean book.
He found a picture of an octopus and read aloud: The octopus tends to be a gentle, shy creature.
Sometimes, though, curiosity gets the best of it and it comes out of hiding.
See, I told you, he’s shy,” said Annie.
He read further: But the octopus has huge strength.
Each of its arms, or tentacles, has many suckers, which act like rubber suction cups.
It is nearly impossible to free an object from their grasp.
“We’ll never get rid of this thing.”
Just then, Jack felt a drop hit his arm.
He looked up at the ceiling.
A thin crack ran along the ceiling.
Smaller cracks branched out from it.
The creature blinked, as if trying to understand her.
The octopus shot a cloud of black liquid into the water and disappeared into the dark cloud.
Its long tentacles trailed through the water.
The mini-sub started to rise slowly again.
“I don’t think so … ” Something bothered Jack.
He looked back at the ocean book.
He read to himself: The octopus squirts black ink to escape its enemies.
One of its main enemies is the shark.
The water was growing clear again.
A shadowy figure moved toward the mini-sub.
The fish was way bigger than the dolphins.
And it had a very weird head.
Jack could feel his heart nearly stop.
The shark swam behind the coral.
said Annie, peering out the window.
“We have to get to the top.”
“Even more water’s coming in,” said Annie, “lots more!”
The water wasn’t dripping now—it was spurting.
“A few seconds, a few seconds,” said Jack.
Suddenly, the mini-sub burst out of the water.
It bobbed on the waves like a cork.
The ocean sparkled all around it.
Jack felt the water rising around his bare feet.
“The octopus must have made cracks in the bottom, too.”
The water was up to their ankles now.
He saw the reef in the distance.
It doesn’t look that far,” he said.
She pressed one of the steering keys.
Then Jack pressed the other pictures.
Now the water was up to their knees.
“I guess we’ll have to swim,” said Jack.
“It’s a good thing we had swimming lessons this summer.”
“And it’s a bad thing we just saw a shark.”
Jack quickly found the picture of the shark in the book.
He read aloud: If you ever see a shark in the water, don’t splash.
“We better do the breast stroke,” said Annie.
He tried to be calm, too.
He calmly took off his glasses.
He calmly put them and the book into his pack.
He calmly put his pack on his back.
She slipped out of the minisub.
Then he calmly lowered himself into the ocean.
He gently pushed the water out of his way as he did the breast stroke.
Then Jack saw something out of the corner of his eye.
A dark fin was zigzagging through the water.
I better not tell Annie, he thought.
She’ll stay calmer if she doesn’t know.
He began to swim faster—then faster.
They both swam as fast, and as calmly, as they could.
Sometimes Annie went even faster than Jack, which made him swim faster.
Jack was so scared that he wasn’t tired at all.
He was swimming for his life—and for Annie’s life, too.
He didn’t look back to see if the shark was still there.
He just kept his eye on the tree house in the distance.
Jack and Annie swam and swam and swam.
It took forever for the tree house to get just a little closer.
Jack realized the reef was farther away than he had thought.
He kept swimming, but his arms and legs felt heavy.
Jack and Annie turned onto their backs.
They floated the way they had learned in swimming class.
We’ll just rest for a minute, Jack thought.
But the more Jack floated, the more tired he felt.
Soon he was too tired even to float.
Something pushed at him in the water.
Had the hammerhead caught up with them?
Jack shut his eyes and waited for the worst.
In front of him was a shiny gray head—a dolphin’s head!
The dolphin pushed Jack with its nose.
She was clinging to the fin of another dolphin!
Her dolphin was moving through the water.
Jack grabbed the fin of his dolphin.
Then the two dolphins swam smoothly through the water, pulling Jack and Annie toward the reef.
The sun shone on the ocean.
His dolphin was taking good care of him.
The dolphins slowed down as they neared the reef.
He let go of the dolphin’s fin and stood up in the water.
Then she threw her arms around her dolphin and gave her a big hug.
And she kissed the dolphin’s nose.
Sukie tossed her head and clicked at Annie.
Then he put his flippers around Jack’s neck.
He threw his arms around the dolphin and gave him a quick kiss.
Sam nodded and made clicking sounds like laughter.
The two dolphins chattered to each other for a moment.
They nodded at Jack and Annie and swam gracefully away.
The dolphins leapt high into the air.
Then they dove back into the water with a SPLASH!
“I wish we could swim like that,” said Jack.
Jack and Annie watched the dolphins until they disappeared.
“I miss them already,” Annie said softly.
He sat down in the shallow water.
The warm water lapped around their shorts and Tshirts.
He took out his glasses and put them on.
“I saw the shark when we were swimming,” Annie said.
I wanted you to stay calm.”
I just swam faster so you would swim faster.”
“And I swam faster so you would swim faster,” said Annie.
“I guess we swam double-fast then,” Jack said.
He shook his head with wonder.
“But we haven’t solved Morgan’s riddle yet,” said Annie.
He pulled his notebook out of his pack.
He pulled out the ocean book.
We’ll never be Master Librarians now.”
Then he started across the pink reef toward the tree house.
Annie bent down to rub her foot.
“Yeah, this … ” She picked up a large gray shell.
Rough and gray as a rock—” “And plain as plain can be!”
The shell looked like a clamshell—only bigger and with more ridges.
“How could this ugly shell be the answer to the riddle?”
“What about the part that says, ‘There’s great beauty in me’?”
He opened the soaked ocean book.
But he was able to turn a few.
He found a picture of the gray shell.
He read: Divers search for oysters in deep water.
But sometimes oysters wash up on reefs or beaches.
Inside some oysters you can find a pearl.
The pearl’s natural beauty makes it a treasure.
“It must have a pearl inside it!”
Annie peered into the crack between the two halves of the shell.
“How does a pearl get in there, anyway?”
Jack read aloud from the wet page: Sometimes a grain of sand will get between the oyster’s shell and its skin.
So it makes a pearly material to surround the grain of sand.
In this way, over a few years, a pearl is formed.
“I can’t tell if there’s a pearl in there or not,” said Annie.
“Maybe we should bang it against a rock,” said Jack.
“Now that would really irritate the oyster,” said Annie.
“Maybe we should just leave it alone,” said Annie.
She gently put the oyster back in the water.
“But how will we know if oyster is the right answer to the riddle?”
Jack pushed his glasses into place.
Then he and Annie picked up their shoes and socks.
They climbed through the window of the tree house.
Morgan’s scroll was lying on the floor.
She and Jack stared at the scroll.
In its place was one shimmering silver word: OYSTER “Morgan’s magic,” whispered Annie.
Jack let out a huge sigh.
“And here’s the Pennsylvania book,” said Annie.
She pointed to a picture of the Frog Creek woods.
The tree house started to spin.
The wind blew harder and harder.
Dawn light slanted into the tree house.
No time at all had passed since they’d left.
Jack rolled up the ancient scroll.
He tucked it into the corner.
“We solved the first riddle,” he said.
“I don’t see another scroll,” said Annie.
“Maybe tomorrow we’ll get the next riddle.”
“I think I need to rest—and dry out.”
His T-shirt and shorts were still soaked.
Only his shoes and socks were dry.
“And this needs to dry out, too,” said Annie.
She put the wet ocean book in a patch of sunlight.
Then Jack and Annie climbed down the ladder.
They walked through the woods, through leafy shadows and golden light.
They left the woods and started down their street.
“You know, we should have found the answer to the riddle right away,” said Jack.
“The oyster was on the reef all along.”
“I know, but we wouldn’t have had so much fun,” said Annie.
“You call being squeezed by an octopus and chased by a shark fun?”
“Don’t forget the dolphins,” Annie said simply.
The dolphins made up for everything.
“I guess they were the true pearl in the oyster,” said Annie.
“I wonder what Sam is doing right now.”
They climbed their steps and went into their house.
Then he and Annie slipped up the stairs to change their clothes.
